claims.text: Maintenance of structural and chemical stability from 473 to 1923 K is primarily governed by configurational entropy and atomic size mismatch.
High configurational entropy and moderate atomic size mismatch suppress phase segregation and ordering.
Suppressing phase segregation and ordering preserves the solid-solution structure and compositional uniformity during thermal cycling.
Nanoparticles containing five or more near-equiatomic metals, exemplified by Co, Ni, Fe, Cu, and Mn, can initially be crystallized as a solid solution.
High configurational entropy lowers the free energy of the solid solution relative to segregated or ordered phases.
Moderate atomic size mismatch prevents rapid diffusion and nucleation of secondary phases.
Insufficient configurational entropy can permit phase segregation or ordering.
Excessive atomic size mismatch can permit phase segregation or ordering.
Phase segregation or ordering causes loss of structural and chemical stability.
High-entropy nanoparticles with moderate atomic size mismatch will retain their initial solid-solution structure after thermal treatment from 473 to 1923 K.
High-entropy nanoparticles with moderate atomic size mismatch will retain a uniform elemental distribution after thermal treatment.
Nanoparticles with lower configurational entropy or extreme atomic size mismatch will show phase separation or ordering relative to the initial baseline.
The initial baseline is a solid solution with uniform elemental distribution and no phase segregation or ordering.

The prediction is restricted to nanoparticles having at least five near-equiatomic metals, high configurational entropy, and moderate atomic size mismatch, treated at 473–1923 K in inert or operationally relevant atmospheres.
Observation of significant phase segregation or ordering in the high-entropy, moderate-size-mismatch set after thermal treatment would falsify the hypothesis.
